name: Day Them / Hoc Them Shadow Education
period: Late 1990s to present (intensified post-2000, major regulatory reforms 2024-2025)
key_figures: Ministry of Education and Training (MOET); public school teachers (primary income supplement); Circular 29/2024/TT-BGDDT authors; Ho Chi Minh City National University (survey); parents as demand drivers
legal_basis: Circular 29/2024/TT-BGDDT (effective February 14, 2025) — regulates private tutoring, prohibits teachers from charging fees to tutor their own students, requires business registration for paid tutoring; Law on Teachers 2025 (No. 73/2025/QH15); fines of 5-50 million VND for violations under existing administrative penalty decrees
political_backdrop: Post-Doi Moi marketization of education created financial pressures on underpaid teachers. The Communist Party emphasizes education as a national priority (Resolution 29-NQ/TW on education reform) but struggles to fund adequate teacher salaries. Political tension between acknowledging tutoring demand and preventing exploitation.
economic_conditions: Vietnam's GDP per capita remains modest (~$4,300 in 2024). Teacher base salary at 2.34 million VND/month (Decree 73/2024, unchanged in 2025 per Resolution 159/2024/QH15). Teachers can earn VND 1-1.5 million per tutoring session/day, often exceeding their monthly official salary in a few days. K-12 tutoring market estimated at $4.8-6.4 billion annually.
international_influences: Shadow education is a pan-East Asian phenomenon — prevalent in South Korea, Japan, China, and other Confucian-influenced societies. UNESCO and World Bank have documented Vietnam's shadow education system. International research (IZA, Springer) has studied the phenomenon extensively.
path_dependencies: Confucian exam culture creates deep demand for competitive academic achievement. Colonial-era French educational structures left hierarchical schooling. Socialist-era centralized curriculum makes standardized testing the primary pathway to university, intensifying tutoring demand. Family investment in education as social mobility strategy is centuries old.
system_design: Teachers provide paid after-school tutoring (day them) to students who seek additional instruction (hoc them). Operates as private enterprise alongside public school system. Three forms: (1) teachers tutoring their own enrolled students (most controversial), (2) teachers tutoring outside students, (3) commercial tutoring centers. Under Circular 29/2024, all paid tutoring requires business registration regardless of scale.
governance: MOET sets national policy; provincial education departments enforce locally. Circular 29/2024 decentralizes some enforcement to school principals who must monitor and report. Hanoi has taken strong action against unauthorized private tutoring. However, enforcement is inconsistent across provinces.
funding_model: Entirely funded by household out-of-pocket payments. No public subsidy for shadow education. Teachers receive direct cash payments from parents. Some schools have circumvented bans by opening 'clubs' that charge fees, blurring the line between school activities and tutoring.
curriculum_approach: Tutoring typically mirrors and reinforces the national curriculum rather than supplementing it. Focus on exam preparation, test-taking techniques, and drilling. Teachers may intentionally underteach in class to create demand for tutoring — a key conflict of interest. Some tutoring covers genuinely advanced content beyond curriculum.
literacy_rates: Vietnam maintains high literacy rates (>95%) across the population. Shadow education contributes to academic performance but literacy gains are primarily attributed to the formal education system and historical campaigns like Binh Dan Hoc Vu.
enrollment_stats: In a HCMU survey, 63.57% of teachers expressed desire to legalize tutoring activities. Private tutoring participation is widespread — even in rural areas, most parents send primary and secondary children to extra study classes. Participation rates are higher in urban areas and increase approaching exam years (Grade 9, Grade 12).
international_rankings: Vietnam's strong PISA performance (ranked 34th of 81 countries in 2022, 2nd in ASEAN after Singapore) is partly attributed to intensive supplementary study. However, PISA scores declined from previous cycles. Some analysts argue shadow education inflates standardized test scores without improving deep learning.
employment_outcomes: [uncertain] Limited direct research linking shadow education participation to employment outcomes. Indirect effect through university admission — tutored students more likely to access competitive universities, which correlates with better employment. However, the skills-gap problem persists regardless of tutoring.
strengths: Addresses legitimate demand for additional academic support. Provides income supplement for chronically underpaid teachers. Enables some students from modest backgrounds to access competitive exam preparation. Flexible and responsive to individual student needs. Creates a market signal about curriculum inadequacy.
weaknesses: Creates perverse incentives for teachers to underteach in public classrooms. Deepens socioeconomic inequality — wealthy families access better tutors. Exhausts students with excessive study hours. Blurs professional boundaries between teacher-as-public-servant and teacher-as-entrepreneur. Enforcement of regulations is weak and inconsistent.
controversies: Teachers tutoring their own students is the most contentious issue — Circular 29/2024 permits it with reporting requirements, sparking public debate. Schools opening 'subject clubs' to circumvent tutoring bans. Parents feel coerced into paying for tutoring to avoid disadvantaging their children. 63.57% of teachers want tutoring legalized, reflecting tension between livelihood needs and educational ethics.
unintended_consequences: Tutoring bans have pushed the market underground, making it harder to regulate. Some schools created fee-based 'clubs' as a workaround. Increased inequality as wealthy families access private centers while poor families lose access to teacher-led tutoring. Student burnout and mental health deterioration from extended study hours. Teacher professional identity crisis.
urban_rural_gap: Urban students have access to higher-quality tutoring centers and specialized tutors. Rural families rely primarily on their school teachers for tutoring — making the conflict of interest more acute. Private tutoring described as 'the only alternative available to rural households' for maximizing education quality. Urban tutoring costs are significantly higher.
ethnic_minority_access: Ethnic minority students in remote areas have minimal access to tutoring services. Language barriers compound the issue. Kinh-majority students in lowland areas benefit disproportionately from shadow education, widening the achievement gap.
gender_disparities: [uncertain] Limited gender-specific data on tutoring participation. General trend suggests similar participation rates for boys and girls in primary/secondary, with some evidence of families prioritizing sons' tutoring in economically constrained households.
disability_inclusion: [uncertain] Shadow education infrastructure is generally inaccessible to students with disabilities. No specific regulations require tutoring centers to accommodate disabled students. Inclusive education policy focuses on formal schooling, not the shadow system.
socioeconomic_stratification: Shadow education is a major driver of educational inequality. Wealthy families spend significantly more on tutoring, creating a two-tier system. International school students ($15,000-30,000/year tuition) access entirely different educational ecosystems. Working-class families may spend 24-47% of household income on education including tutoring.
vs_asean_peers: Shadow education is prevalent across ASEAN but Vietnam's system is distinctive in the teacher-student conflict of interest dimension. Cambodia, Thailand, and Philippines have similar phenomena. Singapore's tuition industry is more commercialized. Vietnam's regulatory approach (Circular 29) is more recent than regional peers.
vs_aspirational_models: South Korea's hagwon (cram school) system is the closest parallel — Korea spent decades trying to regulate it with limited success. Japan's juku industry is similarly entrenched. Finland has virtually no shadow education due to equitable school quality and adequate teacher pay. Singapore has a large commercial tuition industry but less teacher-student overlap.
unesco_framework: Shadow education falls outside formal ISCED classification but operates primarily alongside ISCED levels 1-3 (primary to upper secondary). UNESCO has documented Vietnam's shadow education as part of broader Education for All assessments.
communist_party_goals: Party Resolution 29-NQ/TW (2013) on fundamental education reform acknowledges the need to improve teacher welfare to reduce reliance on tutoring. The Party goal of education equity is undermined by shadow education's stratifying effects. Tension between socialist equality ideals and market-driven tutoring reality.
confucian_legacy: Confucian culture places extreme value on academic achievement and examination success, creating deep-rooted demand for supplementary study. Teacher respect (ton su trong dao) paradoxically enables teachers to leverage their authority for tutoring income. Family obligation to invest in children's education drives parental spending.
modernization_ideology: The Dong Kinh Nghia Thuc (1907) movement emphasized mass education access — shadow education represents a partial failure of this ideal. Phan Chau Trinh's 'khai dan tri' (enlighten the people) vision assumed equitable access, not market-stratified access.
past_reforms: Multiple tutoring bans attempted since the 2000s with limited success. Previous circulars prohibited teachers from tutoring their own students but enforcement was weak. The Education Law 2019 addressed tutoring but lacked specific implementation mechanisms. Each regulatory attempt pushed tutoring underground.
current_initiatives: Circular 29/2024/TT-BGDDT (effective Feb 2025) — most comprehensive regulation yet. Requires business registration for all paid tutoring. Permits teachers to tutor own students with reporting and non-coercion commitments. Fines of 5-50 million VND for violations. Hanoi launched enforcement campaigns in 2025. Law on Teachers 2025 includes provisions for salary improvements to reduce tutoring dependency.
future_vision: Proposed 'special salary coefficient' for teachers (potentially 2026) aims to reduce financial incentive for tutoring. Free digital textbooks by 2029-2030 could reduce overall education costs. EdTech platforms may formalize and regulate tutoring. Long-term goal is adequate teacher compensation eliminating need for moonlighting.
implementation_fidelity: Large gap between policy and practice. Circular 29 acknowledges legitimate demand while trying to prevent abuse — a difficult balance. Enforcement varies dramatically by province. Urban areas see more visible enforcement; rural areas remain largely unmonitored. Schools' 'club' workaround demonstrates creative policy evasion. Teacher salary stagnation (unchanged in 2025) undermines the regulatory framework.
teacher_experience: Teachers earn base salary of 2.34 million VND/month (~$95) — among the lowest professional salaries in Vietnam. Tutoring income of VND 1-1.5 million per day can exceed monthly salary. 63.57% of teachers want tutoring legalized. Teachers face professional reputation risk ('Why do I risk my professional reputation to do it?'). New regulations add compliance burden without addressing root salary issue.
student_experience: Students attend school from 7am-5pm, then tutoring from 6-9pm, often 6-7 days per week. Excessive study hours linked to anxiety, depression, and burnout. Students feel coerced into attending tutoring with their own teacher due to fear of lower grades. Exam pressure (especially Grade 12 university entrance) drives desperate tutoring consumption. Mental health consequences documented in multiple studies.
parent_perspective: Parents feel trapped — not sending children to tutoring risks academic disadvantage. 'Hidden reasons' for paying tutoring fees include maintaining teacher goodwill and social conformity. Education spending consumes 24-47% of household budgets. Parents view tutoring as necessary investment despite financial strain. Some parents explicitly prefer their child's teacher for tutoring continuity.
cultural_attitudes: Education is revered as the primary path to social mobility in Vietnamese culture. 'Ton su trong dao' (respect the teacher) makes questioning tutoring practices socially difficult. Academic achievement is a source of family pride and social status. Society is deeply conflicted — tutoring is both criticized and demanded.
public_spending: Government education spending approximately 6% of GDP (VND 380,561 billion / $14.5 billion in 2024), representing about 15-18% of total government expenditure. However, this is below the targeted 20% of budget allocation. Insufficient public spending on teacher salaries is a root cause of the tutoring phenomenon.
household_spending: Vietnamese families allocate 24-47% of household spending to education. K-12 tutoring market estimated at $4.8-6.4 billion annually (based on 16 million K-12 students, $300-400/student/year). Families spent nearly $4 billion annually on overseas education (2022). Total household education expenditure significantly exceeds public per-student spending.
teacher_compensation: Base salary: 2.34 million VND/month (Decree 73/2024), unchanged in 2025. With allowances and seniority, experienced teachers earn 5-8 million VND/month. Tutoring income: VND 1-1.5 million per day session. Proposed special salary coefficient for teachers anticipated in 2026. Vietnam's teacher pay is among the lowest in ASEAN relative to cost of living.
edtech_market: [uncertain] Vietnam's EdTech market is growing rapidly with startups addressing online tutoring demand. Market size estimated at $3-5 billion by 2025. Platforms like ELSA, Topica, and Marathon Education have received significant investment. EdTech could formalize shadow education or simply extend it into digital spaces.
tutoring_market: Estimated K-12 tutoring market of $4.8-6.4 billion annually. 16 million K-12 students with average parental spending of $300-400/student/year on tutoring. Market encompasses individual teacher tutoring, group classes, commercial centers, and online platforms. Post-Circular 29, market is undergoing formalization with business registration requirements. Urban markets command premium pricing.
test_prep_industry: [uncertain] Commercial exam preparation is a subset of the broader tutoring market. Cram schools targeting university entrance exams (Grade 12) and high school entrance exams (Grade 9) are concentrated in major cities. Some commercial centers operate chains across multiple provinces. IELTS/TOEFL preparation is a growing sub-segment driven by study-abroad demand.
international_school_tier: 21 IB World Schools in Vietnam. International school tuition ranges from $15,000-30,000/year. IB/AP schools serve elite families and expatriates, creating a parallel education system. Students in international schools generally do not participate in the shadow education system as their schools provide comprehensive support. This tier deepens socioeconomic stratification.
